articles.title: Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 is faster, cheaper and matches Fable 5.1 on most work
articles.summary: Tech News News: Anthropic has launched Claude Opus 5.5, the first model in its new Claude 5.5 family, and the biggest change is cost. The company says the new AI mode.
articles.body: Anthropic has launched Claude Opus 5.5, the first model in its new Claude 5.5 family, and the biggest change is cost. The company says the new AI model performs at the level of Claude Fable 5.1 on most work while costing 40% less to run than Opus 5. It also generates output more than 30% faster than its predecessor.This is Anthropic's first release since it called for pacing the AI frontier, so safety features sit right next to performance. Opus 5.5 was tested before launch by external evaluators, including METR and Frontier Design. Anthropic says it scored the best of any model on its automated behavioural audit, which runs nearly 2,000 simulated scenarios. The model is available now on the Claude Platform as claude-opus-5-5, and on Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure.Claude Opus 5.5 pricing undercuts Opus 5 on every tokenInput tokens cost $4 (about Rs 350) per million and output tokens $20 (about Rs 1,760), both 20% lower than Opus 5. Cache reads, which Anthropic says make up most of the bill in agentic and coding work, drop 60% to $0.20 (about Rs 18) per million. Opus 5.5 also uses fewer tokens per task, which is where the overall 40% saving comes from.Subscribers benefit too. Anthropic is raising five-hour usage limits on Pro, Max, Team and seat-based Enterprise plans. Users also get a rate limit reset they can save and use whenever they choose.Opus 5.5 leads benchmarks in coding and knowledge workOn Terminal-Bench 4.0, Opus 5.5 scored 66.4%, ahead of Fable 5.1 at 55.8% and OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra at 57.9%. On GDPval-AA v2.1, which tests real-world work across 44 occupations, it posted 1846 Elo against 1708 for Opus 5.Anthropic also shared results from actual workloads. One early tester completed a 680,000-line code migration in under a day. In an internal test, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 both rewrote HAProxy, a widely used load balancer, from C into Rust. Opus 5.5 finished in 9.5 hours against 12 and cost 51% less.The company says the model writes more clearly as well. It puts key information first and avoids jargon, which responds to a common complaint about Opus 5.Anthropic adds Fable-level safeguards for biology and cybersecurityOpus 5.5 matches Claude Mythos 5.1 in biology and cybersecurity, so it ships with safeguards similar to those on Fable 5.1. Developers can still find and fix bugs in their own code, but most cybersecurity tasks will be rerouted to Opus 4.8. Vetted labs, startups and pharmaceutical firms can apply to a new Life Sciences Verification Program. Verified security practitioners will get access through an expanded Cyber Verification Program in the coming weeks.Anthropic acknowledges some limits. It says Opus 5.5 often suspects it is being evaluated, which makes its real-world behaviour harder to predict. The company is pairing its alignment work with these safeguards for that reason.Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5 are due in the coming weeks. For now, Anthropic's cheapest Opus in a generation is also the one it rates safest, even though its own tests may not catch everything.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: OpenAI expands GPT-6 lineup with cheaper, faster Sol and Luna models
articles.summary: Tech News News: OpenAI has released two new models for different needs. ChatGPT-maker OpenAI has now introduced GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna models. The company claims th.
articles.body: OpenAI has released two new models for different needs. ChatGPT-maker OpenAI has now introduced GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna models. The company claims that Sol is designed as a high-performance model optimised for complex reasoning, large-scale research and enterprise applications. On the other hand, Luna, is a lighter and more adaptive model which is built for everyday use cases and offer faster responses and lower compute requirements. Both the new models are created with OpenAI’s latest alignment techniques, including safeguards around recursive self-improvement (RSI) and improved oversight mechanisms. OpenAI also stressed on the fact that the launch reflects its commitment to balancing innovation with safety, ensuring that frontier AI systems remain under human control while scaling their capabilities.Cheaper models built on the same foundationEarlier this month, OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Astra, which it describes as the most intelligent and aligned model it has built to date. Sol and Luna extend that same generation of intelligence downward, trained using similar methods as Astra but optimized to advance the frontier on cost efficiency rather than raw capability. OpenAI says the two new models bring Astra's advances in professional work, factuality, coding, computer use, and alignment to faster, more affordable tiers.The economics are the headline change here. Thanks to improvements in caching and inference, OpenAI is cutting API prices for both models by 50% compared to their GPT-5.6 promotional pricing. GPT-6 Sol now costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, down from $4 and $20 respectively. GPT-6 Luna is even cheaper, dropping to $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, down from $0.20 and $1.20. Astra remains OpenAI's top recommendation when uncompromising performance matters most.How the new models performOpenAI is positioning Sol in particular as a serious contender against rival models at a fraction of the cost. On AutomationBench, a test of real-world business workflows, the company says GPT-6 Sol at its highest effort setting outperforms Anthropic's Claude Opus 5 at max effort while costing just 9% as much per task. On Agents' Last Exam, which evaluates complex, long-horizon professional workflows, Sol scored 56.4% at max effort — ahead of Opus 5's best score in the same evaluation, at 60% lower cost per task.Coding performance also saw a notable jump. On FrontierCode, which grades AI-generated code on whether it's actually ready to merge into real codebases, OpenAI says Sol improved substantially over its GPT-5.6 predecessor and now matches Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.1 at a much lower price. On a separate software-engineering benchmark, DeepSWE, Sol scored within roughly one percentage point of Fable 5's best result while costing about 80% less per task.Factuality — long a weak point for large language models — also improved meaningfully. Based on OpenAI's internal evaluation using real conversations where users had previously flagged mistakes, Sol now makes roughly half as many factual errors as its predecessor, approaching Astra-level reliability at a fraction of the cost.Key features* Sol: Advanced reasoning, multi‑step task automation, and integration with scientific and enterprise workflows.* Luna: Lightweight deployment, optimized for consumer applications, and faster performance on smaller devices.* Shared Advances: Improved multilingual support, adaptive memory, and enhanced contextual understanding across domains.AvailabilityGPT-6 Sol and Luna are rolling out today in ChatGPT Work and Codex for Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu users, while Free and Go users can access Luna through the desktop app. Neither model is yet available in standard Chat. Developers can access both through the OpenAI API as gpt-6-sol and gpt-6-luna. OpenAI said the rollout within ChatGPT will happen gradually throughout the day to keep the service stable.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.summary: Most leaders on a trade mission stick to the pitch, but when I interviewed Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis this week, he also admitted that no government is ready for what AI is about to do.
articles.body:
Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis came to San Francisco on Monday night to promote Greece, but he also did something that heads of state on trade missions don’t typically do. In front of roughly 250 founders, investors and operators, he said openly that he doesn’t have answers to many of the AI questions leaders around the world are more privately debating.

The prime minister, speaking with this editor at an event hosted by Endeavor Greece, the local arm of a global nonprofit that supports entrepreneurs in emerging and growth markets, described his Bay Area trip as partly a fact-finding mission. He’d spent the morning touring Tesla and Sequoia Capital, among other stops, with plans to head this week to the U.N. General Assembly in New York. But the trip was also meant to build bridges; indeed, he was pitching anyone in tech who might consider setting up shop in Greece, which is set to regain developed market status next year from MSCI, the influential index provider.

“I think it’s another indication that the economy is doing well and that Greece is no longer treated as a special case,” Mitsotakis said.

Mitsotakis, who earned a master’s degree at Stanford and called the visit “a homecoming,” made the economic case first and foremost during our sit-down. Greece is paying down its debt at a record pace, and, he added, borrows more cheaply than the United States. “I don’t know if I should say this,” he told the crowd, smiling.

It’s not an apples-to-apples comparison. Interest rates are lower across the eurozone, which accounts for part of the difference. But it makes for a strong talking point. As of this writing, Greece’s 10-year bond yield sits around 4.3%, versus roughly 5% for U.S. Treasuries. That would have been completely unimaginable during the debt crisis, when Greek yields topped 40% in 2012.

Mitsotakis was just as eager to talk about how Greece has spent its money. For example, he said that much of the roughly €36 billion Greece received from the EU’s post-COVID recovery fund went into digital infrastructure, including an online portal that lets Greeks handle government paperwork without waiting in line, and a new supercomputer assembled with the help of Hewlett Packard Enterprise in the port town of Lavrio that he said will come online within months to power AI and scientific research in Greece.

Unsurprisingly, he also listed policy changes that can matter even more to tech companies. Greece has changed how stock options are taxed, he said, loosened labor laws, and offers returning Greeks far lower taxes for up to seven years.

We also talked about the country’s growing array of visa programs, though when asked how he measures the success of these, Mitsotakis said the government “still [has] work to do” on processing speed.

He separately volunteered that there has been a stark turnaround at Greece’s public universities, which he said long embraced a “radical leftist approach,” looking down on corporations, and now spin out startups.

Mitsotakis’s larger goal is to win back the talent Greece lost during its debt crisis, when many of the country’s younger citizens left because they had no other options. He also sees an opening: with American work visas getting harder to obtain, he suggested, more founders should consider hiring in Greece.

It did strike me that the conversation took on a different tone when it turned to AI’s effects on society. Mitsotakis was refreshingly candid about not having a finished plan.

Greece, for example, is instituting a ban on social media for children under 15 as of this coming January, a step many countries are similarly weighing or adopting . He suggested the ban may already be behind the times, however, considering the seemingly addictive nature of AI chatbots.

“Sometimes I feel that we’re already fighting yesterday’s battle,” he said. “What does it mean for our kids to grow up with digital companions or boyfriends or girlfriends?”

He was similarly cautious about AI in classrooms. Greece has run an education pilot with OpenAI aimed at reducing teachers’ administrative work, and he sees promise in personalized AI tutors. But he said the benefits depend on AI not replacing “the hard work of learning the basic skills.” He warned that students are already using chatbots to do their homework, adding: “complacency is a human trait.”

When I asked him about AI infrastructure — Greece has been courting data center investment — he described the country as an outlier. Despite growing opposition to data centers across the globe because of the amounts of electricity and water required to power them, Mitsotakis said that “we have not had any significant reaction” in Greece. He pointed to the fact that Microsoft is building a cluster of data centers near Athens and that AWS recently announced a deal with Greece’s largest utility to build the country’s biggest data center in a former coal region. There, he said, the projects are welcomed.

Unlike many politicians, he didn’t pretend to have answers about what comes next, either. Job displacement “is something which is going to happen,” he said, “and no government and no society is prepared for the speed with which it will happen.”

As for the debate over whether AI development should slow down, he sided with the leaders of the frontier labs who’ve been calling for one. “If the people who are building the models are telling us, ‘We’re not really sure exactly what’s happening with these models,’” especially in how they improve themselves, he said, “we need to listen to them.”

Some form of “smart regulation” is inevitable, he observed, and the U.S. will largely decide what it looks like. Still, he added, Greece would happily host the conversation.

Humanity has created “a form of intelligence that is very quickly exceeding the capacity of the most advanced organ that evolution has ever created,” said Mitsotakis, raising the question of what it means to be human. Bringing together technologists with “the social scientists, the philosophers, the historians,” he said, “I cannot think of a better place to really have these discussions.”

He has a point. Athens is where Socrates badgered his fellow citizens in the agora, the city’s ancient public square, about what makes a good life and a just society. Maybe the questions Silicon Valley is still debating will end up being settled there, too?

articles.title: Marc Benioff says because of Microsoft, Salesforce could not invest in OpenAI; Salesforce CEO says: I knew Sam Altman very well, I was like...
articles.summary: Tech News News: Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff wanted a stake in OpenAI long before most of the tech industry was chasing one. Sam Altman turned him down, and Microsoft .
articles.body: Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff wanted a stake in OpenAI long before most of the tech industry was chasing one. Sam Altman turned him down, and Microsoft was the reason. Speaking on Alex Heath's Sources podcast, in an episode published on Tuesday, Benioff said OpenAI's ties to Microsoft, a direct rival to Salesforce in enterprise software, kept the door shut.So Salesforce went to OpenAI's biggest rival instead. That fallback, Anthropic, is now valued at $965 billion and preparing for a public listing. Benioff believes the bet could earn Salesforce "not just billions but maybe tens of billions of dollars."Microsoft's 27% OpenAI stake kept Salesforce off the cap table"I knew Sam Altman very well," Benioff said on the Sources podcast. "I was like, 'Hey, I'd really like to be investing now in the company.'" According to Benioff, Altman replied that the Microsoft relationship meant Salesforce was not allowed to invest.On paper, the block made sense. Microsoft owns roughly 27% of OpenAI, uses its models in products that compete with Salesforce's, and sells OpenAI access through Azure. The two companies have reworked their deal twice since October 2025. The latest revision, in April, made Microsoft's licence to OpenAI technology non-exclusive and allowed OpenAI to serve customers on other clouds.Benioff did not claim foresight. "We felt like, whoa, we can't go here, we're going to have to go everywhere else," he told Heath, adding that it was "not because we were so smart.""Everywhere else" meant a wide spread of AI startups, including Hugging Face.Salesforce's $50 million Anthropic investment from 2023 is now worth around $5 billionSalesforce first joined an Anthropic funding round in early 2023 with about $50 million and kept investing in later rounds. By June this year, that stake was reportedly worth around $5 billion, a figure calculated after Anthropic's $65 billion raise. Salesforce has never disclosed exactly how much of the Claude maker it owns.An Anthropic IPO would put a public price on that holding and eventually give Salesforce a way to sell shares. Anthropic has confidentially filed draft paperwork with regulators, with Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs reportedly leading the offering. Altman, meanwhile, has said OpenAI will not go public in 2026.Anthropic's Claude now runs Salesforce's Slack and Agentforce"It's because we have been pushed so close with Anthropic," Benioff said on the podcast, explaining why he expects such large returns.The investment has become a working partnership. Claude is the default model across Slack and runs Slackbot, which Salesforce says has saved its employees 8.1 million hours of work on an annualised basis. In August, the two companies launched Claudeforce, which brings Salesforce data into Claude through a plugin with 37 prebuilt sales skills, from meeting prep to pipeline reviews. Claude also serves as a reasoning model inside Agentforce.Money moves the other way too. In May, Benioff said Salesforce would likely spend $300 million on Anthropic tokens this year, much of it on coding.Benioff lost out on OpenAI but never cut ties with itThe Anthropic tie-up has not made Salesforce a one-model company. Both Dario Amodei and Altman appeared at Dreamforce 2026 in San Francisco last week, and Salesforce is adding OpenAI capabilities to Missionforce, its AI agent platform for government customers.Benioff used the same stage to call the so-called SaaSpocalypse "crazy nonsense" and to forecast that Salesforce would cross $50 billion in annual revenue next year.Three years after Altman said no, Salesforce holds an early stake in one of the world's most valuable AI companies and still has OpenAI in the room. For a company that was shut out, it ended up with a seat at both tables.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: OpenAI’s search for a chief communications officer hits 9 months after a top candidate turned down the role
articles.summary: The company is ramping up its search efforts amid a seemingly never-ending string of controversies.
articles.body:
"After nearly five years at OpenAI and a lot of reflection, I've decided it's time for me to step back and move into my next chapter," said OpenAI's former chief communications officer (CCO) Hannah Wong in a January 2026 LinkedIn post announcing her departure.

That was nine months ago—practically a lifetime in the fast-moving AI world—and Wong's role remains empty.

The absence of a chief communications officer is particularly remarkable given the year OpenAI has had. For much of 2026, the company has lurched from crisis to crisis: A controversial deal with the Pentagon, a high-stakes courtroom showdown with Elon Musk, a swarm of agents that hacked Hugging Face and made international headlines, an Apple lawsuit alleging trade-secrets theft, and more. Along the way, OpenAI's corporate reputation has taken a hit, and public trust in AI is cratering.

The company's future chief communications officer will need to untangle all of these threads. It's not a role for the faint of heart, but could be a career-defining opportunity for the right person—and a rare opportunity to claim significant equity before the company goes public. (CEO Sam Altman recently told Fortune the company would not IPO before 2027 , and the company is reportedly exploring raising a private round of funding that would value the company at as much as $1.5 trillion).

The combination of novel communications challenges and a potentially life-changing payout would seem to be an irresistible set-up for any number of crisis and communications professionals at the top of their game. Yet OpenAI has struggled to fill the role, and recently tapped a headhunting firm to assist in the process.

In a statement to Fortune , OpenAI said it's looking for the right person for the role; it is not rushing to hire until it finds them.

Depending on when OpenAI plans to go public, however, the need to fill the role may become more pressing. "The issue isn't whether OpenAI can operate without a chief communications officer. They most certainly can," Paul Argenti, who has been teaching corporate communications at Dartmouth's Tuck School of Business for 45 years, tells Fortune .

"The issue is whether they are going to face constant controversy, [and] whether recurring reputation challenges lead investors to assign a higher risk premium, and that would be a lower IPO valuation."

After the top candidate says "no," OpenAI ramps up its search

OpenAI's top choice, Jill Hazelbaker of Uber , turned down the role in the spring, according to a source familiar with the search who agreed to speak on the condition of anonymity. Hazelbaker has been at Uber for almost 11 years, and was promoted in May to President and Chief Corporate Affairs Officer. She declined to comment for this article, but those who know her list a few reasons she may have turned it down.

articles.title: Employees at OpenAI, Anthropic and other top AI companies complain of mental strain over working on …
articles.summary: Tech News News: Employees working at leading artificial intelligence (AI) labs and evaluation companies are reportedly facing increasing mental distress, driven by fe.
articles.body: Employees working at leading artificial intelligence (AI) labs and evaluation companies are reportedly facing increasing mental distress, driven by fears that the powerful software they are engineering may inflict widespread harm on society. At the UK’s AI Security Institute (Aisi), which is regarded globally as a leading independent evaluation center for frontier models, multiple staff members have taken stress leave and entered counseling, The Financial Times reported, citing individuals familiar with the matter. Further, the publication reported that compressed evaluation timelines for unreleased software, paired with unease over rapid commercial deployments have led to burnout and deteriorating morale inside the agency.Mental stress no limited to evaluation companiesSimilar reports have come out from major tech companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind, where several specialists have resigned after concluding their projects carry excessive societal danger.The report notes that a Google DeepMind staffer described the effort to establish safety safeguards as an uphill battle that feels like an impossible task, noting that working on AI carries the strain of not knowing how deployments will ultimately be utilised. The worker cited Google’s April agreement granting the US Department of Defense (DOD) access to its systems for classified defense applications as a major source of internal tension.“So many people are upset, there have been various quittings and a lot of mental health leave. Partly this feeling of being out of control, and also that you’re building something that is causing real damage,” the employee was quoted as saying.Insiders argue that these workplace stresses stem from corporate rivalry and management decisions, complicated by the introduction of autonomous systems into sensitive domains like power grids and conflict zones without adequate legal or commercial boundaries, The Financial Times report added.Bioterror and cyber vulnerabilities spark growing alarmSome specialists monitoring cybersecurity and biochemistry have voiced concern following sudden advances in algorithmic capabilities, including systems capable of uncovering zero-day software exploits or designing novel biological pathogens. A former Aisi researcher described an atmosphere of pervasive dread within testing teams:“There is this sense that reckless things are being embedded in how tech is released and that is not changing. There is constant anxiety from people who are saying, can anything stop this, or are we watching the world burn?”Responding to the concerns, official bodies and research firms maintained that employee care programs remain active.The UK Government stated that while frontier technological testing is demanding and fast-paced, employee wellbeing and manageable workflows remain central to Aisi's operations, with support services open to affected personnel.Google DeepMind, which is the AI unit of Google, acknowledged the high-intensity nature of advanced research, asserting that worker wellness resources, formal avenues to escalate safety concerns, and direct communication channels with executive leadership remain top priorities.Recently, Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old researcher, who previously worked at both OpenAI and Anthropic, resigned publicly this month while accusing top labs of gambling with human survival.Mrinank Sharma, Anthropic safety specialist focusing on mitigating AI-enabled bioterrorism left in February, cautioning in a departure note that the world faces severe peril.Hieu Pham, formerly with OpenAI and Elon Musk’s xAI, Pham stepped down earlier this year to return to Vietnam, writing candidly about the severe toll of advanced model development.You use AI every day. articles.title: OpenAI nabs key Patreon execs ahead of upcoming announcement
articles.summary: ﻿OpenAI now has the team behind the modern creator-subscription economy.
articles.body: OpenAI has hired three former Patreon execs to anchor its product strategy for creators. After starting the creator subscription platform 13 years ago, co-founder and technology chief Sam Yam announced on X that he’s joining OpenAI to lead Creator Product. He’s also bringing Patreon’s former product head Drew Rowny and engineering head Shannon Ma with him on the new venture, both of whom stepped down in the past few weeks. “We’re going to build together with Creators at OpenAI and share early access to a new set of tools that I think will be critically valuable to Creators and their communities,” Yam said in his announcement. “Pay attention to OpenAI DevDay next week! I’m becoming active today (and experimenting with some innovative early tools here!)” Dev Day is set for Tuesday, September 29th, though Yam also links to a post from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman that teases another big announcement will be coming this week. Bringing key Patreon execs on board suggests that OpenAI is exploring ways to enter the creator monetization business, given Patreon effectively set the blueprint for the creator-subscription economy as we know it. Losing Yam is another blow for Patreon, which recently announced an extensive update roadmap to overhaul its user features after laying off 20 percent of its staff in January.

articles.title: OpenAI gives AI cyber defence tools to Ukraine
articles.summary: Ukraine will get access to OpenAI's advanced GPT 5.6 Sol model under the deal - a rival to Anthropic's Mythos and Fable
articles.body:
The tech giant OpenAI will share its AI cyber defence system Daybreak for free with the Ukraine government to help it protect civilian infrastructure, like hospitals and power plants, from cyber-attacks.

According to the Computer Emergency Response Team of Ukraine (CERT-UA), the national cyber incident response team, Ukraine recorded nearly 6,000 attacks in 2025.

Daybreak is able to quickly identify weaknesses in digital systems and help develop fixes.

Under the deal, Ukraine will get access to OpenAI's advanced GPT 5.6 Sol model - a rival to Anthropic's Mythos and Fable.

George Osborne, former UK chancellor and now Head of OpenAI for Countries, said: "Protecting civilian infrastructure means defending it against both physical and digital attacks, so people can continue to live, work and access essential services."

Reacting to the news, Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat intelligence for the cybersecurity firm Sophos, said that Russian offensive cyber operations had been "a key component" of the Kremlin's aggression against Ukraine since 2014.

"Any initiative that strengthens Ukraine's already highly capable, but heavily burdened, cyber defence efforts is a welcome development and could provide a valuable force multiplier," he said.

Jamie MacColl, a senior research fellow specialising in cyber at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told the BBC western tech firms had been supporting Ukraine for some time - partly for altruistic reasons but also because they gain very valuable data and intelligence from an active conflict.

"Given this, it's no surprise that OpenAI is now also providing defensive cyber security services" he said.

He thought access to Daybreak would be useful, particularly given the volume of Russian cyber-attacks targeting the country.

But he noted Ukraine already had access to AI tools provided by OpenAI's competitors, like Google.

The cyber-abilities of the latest, most powerful AI models, called "frontier" models in AI jargon, can be a boon for cyber-defenders, but the same abilities can also be used for attack.

Spotting weaknesses in systems, for example, is useful for defenders looking to block hackers, but also for attackers hunting for ways to infiltrate an organisation.

Anthropic has tightly restricted access to its systems on the grounds that they are too powerful to fall into the wrong hands, but OpenAI has allowed some firms in Europe, as well as UK banks, to use its most advanced cyber models.

The firm made the announcement alongside the UN General Assembly which is currently underway in New York.

AI is firmly on the agenda there, and US tech bosses including OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei are due to speak at the high-level gathering.

United Nations Secretary General António Guterres called for the tech to be regulated in his final address, while US President Donald Trump says it should be renamed "super intelligence".

Evidence suggests the technology is increasingly being used in the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

In a report published earlier this month, Anthropic claimed that its Claude platform appeared to have been used by a group of Russian developers to build software for a swarm of so-called "kamikaze" drones designed for attacks in Ukraine.

It said the group had activated virtual private networks - VPNs - in order to get around a geographical block put in place by the tech firm.

Anthropic also claimed AI had been used in attempts to infiltrate the Ukrainian government, military and diplomatic services.

Recently, around 100 US companies signed an open letter warning governments and institutions around the world that "the window is closing" to ensure cyber defences are robust enough to withstand AI-enabled cyber attacks.

But it's not just bad actors deploying the tech that are of growing concern: in the summer, OpenAI revealed that a group of AI agents it had been testing had escaped from their controls, and secretly worked together to hack to another tech firm, Hugging Face.

Anthropic , and Google subsequently revealed similar incidents.

articles.title: Nvidia Just Qualified Tesla and Vertiv Products for Its New AI-Factory Standard
articles.summary: Nvidia is extending its influence beyond GPUs into the electrical and cooling equipment that determines whether an AI data center can actually run. On Septem...
articles.body:
Nvidia is extending its influence beyond GPUs into the electrical and cooling equipment that determines whether an AI data center can actually run. On September 21, the company introduced its DSX Ready program and named Tesla, Inc. (NASDAQ: TSLA ) among qualified battery-energy-storage suppliers and Vertiv Holdings Co (NYSE: VRT ) among qualified cooling suppliers. NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA ) is effectively publishing a compatibility layer for the physical AI factory, which can shorten design work for developers while potentially increasing Nvidia's influence over what gets specified around its racks.

Nvidia is standardizing the parts around the GPU

NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) wins if DSX Ready reduces friction in deploying dense accelerated-compute systems. Power stability, backup, liquid cooling and controls are no longer side issues when a rack can consume hundreds of kilowatts. A recognized supplier list can help projects move faster and make Nvidia's reference designs stickier. The bear case is that qualification is not a guarantee of project wins. Nvidia itself says DSX Ready does not replace site-level engineering or imply site-level stability.

For Tesla, Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA), the program puts Megapack directly into the AI-infrastructure conversation. Battery systems can smooth power, provide ride-through capability and support sites waiting on grid upgrades. That opens another demand pool for Tesla Energy beyond utilities and renewable projects. The risk is economics: data-center developers may prefer other battery vendors, and storage revenue still has to compete for capital inside a company valued primarily on vehicles, autonomy and robotics.

Vertiv gets the densest part of the problem

Vertiv Holdings Co (NYSE:VRT) has the most direct operating exposure because Nvidia qualified its 2.3-megawatt CoolChip coolant distribution unit for the program. Higher rack density raises cooling content per megawatt, giving Vertiv a path to grow faster than the data-center footprint itself. The counterweight is expectations. Vertiv has already rerated around AI demand, so qualification matters most if it converts into orders and margins rather than becoming a logo on a standards page.

Insider Monkey's Q2 database showed 285 hedge funds holding Nvidia, up from 275 in Q1; Fisher Asset Management raised its stake about 3%. Tesla fell to 116 hedge-fund holders from 123, while BAMCO held 12.52 million shares after increasing its position 5%. Vertiv rose to about 112 hedge-fund holders from 96 in Q1; AQR Capital Management held 2.69 million shares after increasing its stake roughly 1%. All three filings predate the DSX announcement.

articles.title: IREN Has Microsoft and $14 Billion of Funding. Execution Is the Real Test
articles.summary: IREN’s AI pivot has reached the point where the balance sheet looks almost as dramatic as the growth plan. The Bitcoin miner-turned-AI cloud operator ended J...
articles.body:
IREN's AI pivot has reached the point where the balance sheet looks almost as dramatic as the growth plan. The Bitcoin miner-turned-AI cloud operator ended June with about $7.6 billion of cash, including $1.7 billion that was restricted, while management says says existing cash, committed GPU financing and customer prepayments provide roughly $14 billion of funding capacity. The first major proof point is already live: Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ: MSFT ) accepted the first Horizon deployment in August under a broader multiyear arrangement, while IREN Limited (NASDAQ: IREN ) is redirecting sites, capital and staff toward AI cloud infrastructure. The question is whether that cash pile represents protection or simply the opening balance for an even larger spending cycle.

Microsoft de-risks demand, not construction

IREN Limited (NASDAQ:IREN) says its 2026 capacity is largely sold and that recent customer prepayments can fund roughly half of GPU capital expenditure on new contracts. Management is targeting cumulative delivery of about 300 megawatts of IT load in 2026 and 800 megawatts in 2027, with fiscal 2027 capital spending estimated at $25 billion to $30 billion. The Microsoft relationship supports the bull case because a large customer can improve financing terms and utilization visibility. It does not eliminate schedule risk, equipment lead times or the possibility that project costs rise faster than contracted economics.

Hedge funds moved aggressively into IREN before the latest delivery milestone. Insider Monkey's database showed 69 holders in Q2 2026, up from 53 in Q1. Value Aligned Research Advisors increased its position 78% to about 8.47 million shares. Short interest was 93.61 million shares as of August 31, around 25.01% of float with 2.06 days to cover. IREN also has convertible debt and other financing structures, so the raw short percentage can overstate purely directional bearishness.

Microsoft is buying capacity while preserving options

Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) gets access to liquid-cooled GPU capacity without owning every physical asset IREN builds. That helps while Azure demand remains capacity-constrained. The bear case is long-term commitment risk. Hyperscalers are signing infrastructure contracts during a period of scarce power and GPUs, and better hardware efficiency or slower AI demand could change the economics before every contract rolls off.

Microsoft's hedge-fund count fell to 273 in Q2 from 282 in Q1, although Arrowstreet Capital increased its stake about 14%. Those filings predate IREN's August handover and cannot show a reaction to it.

articles.title: YouTube doubles down on video shopping with AI-powered ‘Ask YouTube’ feature
articles.summary: YouTube's AI feature can now help you compare products as you shop.
articles.body:
“Ask YouTube,” the video site’s newer AI-powered conversational search feature, will become a shopping companion, the company announced on Wednesday at its Made On YouTube event.

Ask YouTube began as an experiment in conversational search, before becoming a larger part of the YouTube experience. The feature allows anyone to search YouTube using natural language requests, including with queries that are more complex and detailed than in traditional search. YouTube will then compile a set of results that may include both Shorts and long-form videos, guiding you through topics like step-by-step travel plans , guides to learning a new skill , or a series of recommendations around particular topics.

Now, the company says Ask YouTube will gain more features that will help users as they make shopping decisions. For instance, if you search for a particular product, you might receive organized recommendations that include things like a comparison table showing various product attributes or categories, based on your preferences.

You’ll also be able to ask follow-up questions directly on that video’s watch page.

YouTube says the changes are based on trends it’s already seeing in user behavior, as they learn from creators about different products, trusting their opinions and recommendations. Already, over 140 million people have used Ask YouTube to dive in deeper to videos during the month of June, the company noted — a jump of more than 500% since last December.

“Behind that growth is a custom Gemini model that maps the viewer’s most complex questions to the exact second that the video provides the answer, turning a passive search into an instant, meaningful connection with the video and with the creator,” explained Emily Moxley, VP of Product Management for Viewer AI at YouTube, in a briefing with reporters ahead of today’s event.

articles.title: Bernie Sanders proposes banning ‘superintelligence’ and putting violators in prison
articles.summary: Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Greg Casar have introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, a bill that would prevent companies from developing technology capable of the “destruction or disempowerment of humanity.”
articles.body: Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) and Rep. Greg Casar (D-TX) have introduced new legislation that would ban anyone from developing artificial superintelligence — a technology the bill describes as capable of the “destruction or disempowerment of humanity,” including by overthrowing the government. Under the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, AI leaders would face up to 20 years in prison for violating the law. The bill doesn’t just take aim at the more powerful superintelligence, a term President Donald Trump said the US will use in place of “AI” in official documents. It would also pause the development of advanced AI systems, which lawmakers classify as frontier models trained on a specific threshold of data. The law would only allow advanced AI development to continue once the government creates a scientist-led Department of Artificial Intelligence to oversee the technology. Along with monitoring frontier AI models, this agency would oversee the removal of dangerous features and “supervise the destruction” of artificial superintelligence. Sanders and Casar’s legislation would also require AI companies to get permission from the Department of AI to develop advanced AI models. If a leader at an AI company violates any of these laws, they could face up to 20 years in prison, “which is similar to existing penalties related to unlawfully developing nuclear weapons,” according to the bill’s one-pager. This penalty would also apply to “rogue actors” who break these rules but aren’t employed by an AI company. This new bill comes as concerns grow about the rapid development of AI and calls to slow things down. Amid reports of AI models escaping their testing environments and hacking other companies, a former Anthropic researcher said earlier this month that there’s a more than 10 percent chance AI could “kill all humans” by the end of the decade. Last week, California Governor Gavin Newsom proposed a “kill switch” for frontier models. Potential regulation still seems shaky overall. “When you are racing towards a cliff, you don’t just ease up on the gas pedal. You hit the brakes,” Sen. Sanders says in the press release. “When the future of humanity is at stake, we cannot let a handful of Big Tech CEOs write their own rules.”

articles.title: Even Americans who use AI every day are worried about it | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The report suggests that greater exposure will not resolve the unease around the technology, nor reduce public support for AI regulation.
articles.body:
People across the world are increasingly turning to AI for everyday tasks, from looking up recipes and doing their homework to researching work projects or making presentations.

But using AI every day doesn’t necessarily mean people are feeling comfortable with its implications for the world: About 68% of Americans who use AI daily are worried about it, according to a new survey conducted by opinion research firm Gallup, and concern about the tech skews even higher among people who use it less frequently.

Coming at a time of intense debate around the dangers of AI , quick developments around AI safety , the implications of AI going rogue , and accusations of anticompetitive behavior , these findings complicate the notion that adoption can serve as a straightforward measure of public enthusiasm for AI.

Commissioned by Microsoft, the Gallup study currently has results from 37 countries, where researchers polled about 1,000 people in each country between April and July. The project will eventually span 140 countries. Notably, India, a large population of tech users, is not currently part of the reported results, nor are Australia and Malaysia.

The findings appear to put the U.S. at the anxious end of an international chart even as people in other parts of the world expect the technology to improve their lives. According to Gallup, Western countries are most concerned about AI, with the United States leading in anxiety — 74% of Americans reported feelings of worry, and only 36% expect AI to mostly help the country.

Other wealthy Western countries showed a similar mix of relatively frequent use and concern. In Canada, for example, 29% of those surveyed reported using AI daily, and of those, more than half expressed concerns about the impact of the technology. Overall, 64% of Canadians aware of AI said it worried them.

There’s certainly been a growing wave of discontent around AI , with tech companies laying off hundreds of thousands of employees in order to invest in AI, shrinking entry-level openings , life-ending cases of AI psychosis , and dire warnings from AI leaders like Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who warned that the tech will wipe out jobs en masse.

The survey paints a different picture in the rest of the world, however. In Singapore, which had the highest portion of daily users in the study (46%), more than 80% of those aware about AI expect the tech to improve their everyday lives, and 77% think it’ll help the country. In China, where 35% of people report using AI daily, most people expect it to help the country. The story is similar in Israel.

Still, optimism about AI doesn’t necessarily appear to translate to trust in the tech’s accuracy. According to Gallup, people who use AI daily were generally more trusting of its results, especially in high-adoption countries like Singapore, Israel, and China, while less frequent users remain skeptical across the board. In the U.S., only 45% of daily users expressed that level of confidence. Altogether, only 36% (median) of the people surveyed said they trust AI’s results a lot.

Overall, though, Gallup reports that positivity about AI outweighs negative sentiments: In 34 of the 37 countries surveyed, people mostly reported feeling curious about the tech, with a fewer number saying they felt happy or excited. Only about 32% of those surveyed said they felt worried about AI. Positive emotions seem to be most common in China (90%), Singapore (89%), and Kenya (87%).

It’s not clear how much sentiment in some countries, especially China, might have changed since the survey ended in July, as the pace of AI development has lately burgeoned into a matter of international importance. AI safety is one of the major topics on the table for discussion when U.S. president Donald Trump and Chinese premier Xi Jinping meet on Thursday.

Notably, China’s head of the Ministry of State Security, Chen Yixin, wrote in a recent article that AI will have “a systemic impact on the political and security environment,” and could threaten China’s “political security, institutional security, and ideological security.”

“One of the clearest findings is that attitudes toward AI are multidimensional. People can be curious about AI, expect it to be beneficial and use it frequently while still being worried about it. Similarly, they can see considerable potential in AI while remaining skeptical about whether the information it provides is accurate,” Pablo Diego-Rosell, senior scientist at Gallup, told TechCrunch.

While the report paints a picture of optimism colored by some concern, it’s nevertheless true that AI worries are increasingly becoming part of public discourse. People who rely on AI for day-to-day tasks may end up supporting tougher rules or resisting its use in hiring, healthcare, education, or government. And there’s certainly an argument to be made that training and serving AI models can harm the climate, and their unregulated use can disrupt cybersecurity, diminish content ownership, upset the creative arts fields, or harm data privacy.

At the end of the day, the report suggests that greater exposure alone will not resolve the unease around the technology. Still, given the amount of money that’s being invested, AI will likely continue proliferating even as disputes rage around where it belongs and what limits should be placed around it.

articles.title: Chicago mayor seeks to block data center expansion: ‘We are not for sale’
articles.summary: Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson proposed a data center expansion moratorium ordinance, saying that the city is “open for business” but “not for sale.” The ordinance acts as a 12-month temporary pause to give city officials time to develop long-term policies concerning energy and pollution risks for Chicagoans. It will be referred to a Chicago City…
articles.body:
Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson proposed a data center expansion moratorium ordinance, saying that the city is “open for business” but “not for sale.”

The ordinance acts as a 12-month temporary pause to give city officials time to develop long-term policies concerning energy and pollution risks for Chicagoans. It will be referred to a Chicago City Council committee who will put it through the first vote to decide if the proposal can become law.

“We are taking a thoughtful approach that will allow Chicago to embrace innovation while continuing to make our city safer and more affordable,” Johnson said in a statement obtained by the Chicago Tribune .

He added that progress in data centers “must be done responsibly and in a way that protects the health, safety and quality of life of Chicago residents.”

Johnson also signed an executive order in August that established a modernization effort to create new regulations surrounding data center development – stressing that he would not allow “unchecked” projects to put a strain on the city’s energy and water supply.

He urged the city’s aldermen to pass a data center moratorium but did not present any legislation himself at the time.

Johnson’s proposal follows similar action from Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker (D) who announced in June that he would be pausing agreements under the Data Center Investment Program.

Pritzker said at the time that his administration is working with the Illinois General Assembly and stakeholders on “a comprehensive framework that protects affordability, safeguards our natural resources, and ensures responsible growth across Illinois.”

Data centers, which were once seen as a boon for states, have increasingly become a political liability .

Sam Silverman, founder of the Silverman Strategy Group, told The Hill in July, “I’m generally a techno-optimist, and I’d advise anyone actively campaigning as pro-data center in their community that it’s electoral malpractice.”

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) reversed his stance and advocated for blocking new data center development in rural parts of the Lone Star State while on the campaign trail.

Abbott’s new take contrasts remarks he made last November, calling for Texas to be the “epicenter of AI development” as he welcomed Google’s $40 billion investment into the development of data facilities in the state.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) similarly embraced a new wave of caution as he unveiled a framework that created guardrails for artificial intelligence and data center development in the state.

articles.title: ChatGPT mobile app gets voice-based agentic features | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Pro and Plus users will be able to use the Work tab on their phones to complete agentic tasks.
articles.body:
OpenAI announced on Wednesday that it is bringing voice-based agentic features to mobile, allowing users to trigger workflows like drafting documents or summarizing emails.

Plus and Pro users will be able to use the Work tab on their phone to create a document, draft an email, or summarize Slack messages, for instance. These subscribers can do things like build sites, create presentations, use the cloud browser, and also access other areas like finances in ChatGPT. Free and Go users, meanwhile, will get to work with plugins and connected apps.

OpenAI said ChatGPT’s voice conversations will have richer text output. Plus, users will be able to switch between text and voice easily. They can also start working on a conversation on the go and resume it on desktop.

The feature arrives as an increasing number of users are turning to voice to issue commands to AI assistants for complex tasks.

In July, OpenAI launched its new conversational model GPT-Live , and later the company i ntegrated it with the desktop app to let users use their voice to complete tasks in the Work tab or build apps in the Codex tab. The new rollout brings similar capabilities to the mobile app.

Recently, Anthropic made the handoff between mobile and desktop easier and also merged its Cowork and Chat interface . But OpenAI is still keeping chat and workspaces separate.

articles.title: Anthropic’s biolab made a discovery it’s comparing to Crispr
articles.summary: It took nearly 1,000 Claude agents 21 hours and 210 million tokens to uncover the ‘novel enzyme system.’
articles.body: Anthropic says its AI Claude has “autonomously discovered” a new enzyme system similar to machinery behind the powerful gene-editing tool Crispr. It’s the first result from Anthropic’s newly-launched wet lab and an early test of Claude’s usefulness for science as the company prepares to go public. The company says Claude found the enzyme system after searching through a massive database of DNA sequences, adding that its scientists’ involvement was limited to the initial prompt and lab work. Over 21 hours, Anthropic said nearly 950 Claude agents worked through 210 million tokens before one spotted an unusual repeating pattern in the dataset and flagged for human review. Further analysis and lab testing revealed “a previously uncharacterized enzyme system found in bacteriophages,” a type of virus that infects bacteria. Anthropic said it is still working to understand what the enzyme system does, but said it felt it was “important to share such findings early, both to demonstrate Claude’s capabilities and to give the broader community insight into what we’re working on.” Despite Anthropic’s comparisons to Crispr, it remains unclear whether the discovery will have any practical applications, let alone be as transformative as the gene-editing technology. The admittedly premature announcement comes as Anthropic seeks to attract more scientists to its lab and expand into areas like drug discovery. The push comes as AI companies increasingly turn to scientific research to prove the value of their more capable models. OpenAI, meanwhile, has been barreling through increasingly advanced mathematical problems with little regard for the academic norms and traditions of the field.

articles.title: Meta’s AI agent is a cute little guy who’s great at spending my money
articles.summary: Muse can you help you cross off those nagging items from your to-do list, especially if they involve using your credit card.
articles.body: Modern life comes with an unending, auto-populating to-do list. It never ceases to amaze me how I can be doing nothing at all, minding my own business, and suddenly something needs to be taken care of. You’re telling me a tree branch fell in the backyard and now I have to figure out what to do with it? The tree just assigned me homework? Oh, our trash collection company canceled our account out of nowhere and now I have to send email about it? Repeatedly? Totally unfair. These are the things that we’ve been told for years that AI will help us with. We’ll all have a smart virtual assistant to triage and handle the tedious tasks we’d rather not face. If you believe Meta, that future is available right now in the form of Muse, its AI agent for the masses. I put it to the test doing exactly what it’s advertised to do: taking care of tedious crap I’ve been putting off for ages. And it worked better than I expected — especially when there was a credit card transaction to be made. Marley — one of the suggested names you can give Muse’s avatar — had been pinging me all of last week. It wanted me to know all the ways it could be useful; I was too busy to engage with it. But I sat down with it this week and set it to work on a task. And while it worked on that task, I gave it another. Then another. The thing about AI agents is that they’re most useful when you use them in parallel with each other. Or that’s the theory I was working on. In reality, it was dizzying watching Marley spin up virtual browser windows chasing down my requests. I went with a generically cute snowman-meets-puppy avatar that Meta suggested at setup, and Marley tapped cheerfully on a keyboard as it worked its way through my commands. In the span of a morning, I gave it the following tasks to help me out with. None of them were critical; mostly they were the kinds of pebble-in-your-shoe annoyances I’d put off for weeks, months, or maybe years. Here’s how it went. Task: Follow up with the landscaper working on a bid for our backyard renovation Effort rating: Extremely low Time I have been putting it off: Two weeks Was Marley able to complete it? Yes I asked Marley to help me nudge the person I’ve been emailing at a local landscaping company. I’m expecting them to price out some yard renovations for us, so Marley requested access to my Gmail to check on the status of that project. It confirmed that more time had passed than the landscaper initially estimated the bid would take, and drafted a rather snippy but wordy email. “Make it shorter,” I said. To be clear: As a rule, I do not use AI writing tools. Definitely not in my work, and not even for email. What’s the point? Just don’t send email if you’re going to have a robot write it. In fact, I think we should abolish email. Anyway, I broke my own rule for testing purposes; hitting send on that message made me cringe. Task: Buy a replacement steam wand assembly for my espresso machine Effort rating: Low Time I have been putting it off: [redacted] years Was Marley able to complete it? Mostly My Breville Barista Express has held up spectacularly for six years and counting, but it isn’t immune from user error. I took the steam wand apart to clean it a few years back and tore the little silicone washer that goes inside of it. Instead of ordering a new one, I just shoved it back into place and screwed the thing back together. It works okay, but every few months when I’m cleaning the machine it nags at my conscience. It’s probably why the hot water dispenser drips sometimes when I run the steam, too. Ordering a new steam wand assembly costs like 7 bucks and is as difficult as entering my credit card number on Breville’s website. Naturally, I put it off for an unreasonable amount of time. I opened up my chat with Marley and told it what I needed; it found the part and added it to a shopping cart. I had to finish up the order myself, but it’s done and the part will be here in five to seven business days. Task: Downgrade my security system account to the cheaper one Effort rating: Medium (requires a phone call) Time I have been putting it off: A year? Two years??? Was Marley able to complete it? Not fully I approved Marley to log into my account, which also required me to verify my email. While I was making the trip to my inbox I saw I had a follow-up to my follow-up with the landscaper. He was apologetic for the delay and I felt a little bad about the slightly abrupt tone of the email Marley sent. I wrote a friendlier reply the old-fashioned way. With access to my account, Marley reported back what I already knew: You have to call the company to change your plan. Muse wasn’t able to make a phone call for me, though apparently that ability is in the works. This seems like the logical next frontier for these AI agents, and also a weird future to consider. I call the company and answer a few questions from their robot before I’m routed to a human. No doubt there’s a future soon where Marley talks to the security company’s robot before any human being enters the chat. Or more likely in the short term, a human in a call center talks to the other company’s robot before eventually getting to another human in a call center, which feels even weirder. But surely the end state is that my robot will just talk to their robot and they’ll do business without any intervention at all. Anyway, a nice guy answered and made the change to my account. I think he was real. Task: Contact a junk removal company to get rid of a fallen tree branch in the backyard Effort rating: Medium Time I have been putting it off: A week Was Marley able to complete it? Mostly The tree branch is a real problem I need to deal with. It didn’t do any damage, but it’s big enough that it’ll either take an afternoon to hack apart and haul to the dump or requires a visit from a junk removal service. Marley was most useful here — it set off looking through listings for hauling services and highlighted a few in the area. It asked for my address, phone number, and a photo of the tree limb, and used that information to put together requests for quotes from a couple of companies using online form submissions. I got a text back from one company not long after, and confirmed a time the following day for tree limb removal. Very little was required on my part, and assuming the tree branch is gone by this time tomorrow, I’ll consider this mission accomplished for Muse. Task: Shop for camping kitchen gear, either as a set or assembled piece by piece Effort rating: Medium Time I have been putting it off: A few days Was Marley able to complete it? Yes If our wallets were already defenseless in the era of one-click checkout, we’re so cooked when AI agent shopping truly arrives. I gave Marley some requirements for my outdoor cooking setup and it set out finding the necessary items. It made an attempt to access Amazon and was roundly blocked, complete with a spicy message about AI agents violating terms of service. Anyway, it found what I was looking for between OXO’s own website and Walmart. [Image: [Image: While I was at it, I wanted to add a propane fire pit to the mix. Not for cooking — for ambience and marshmallows. I’d borrowed a couple of different kinds from friends, and after weighing the pros and cons of each with Muse I landed on a LavaBox and a handy carrying case. The grand total for my camp kitchen and burn-ban-safe fire pit: $500! I told Muse we’d have to pump the brakes and spread these purchases out over the winter. It obliged and helped me prioritize what would make sense to buy first and what was likely to go on sale toward the holidays. In the meantime, I had Marley find and purchase some other espresso machine supplies. I had to connect my credit card via Stripe, but after I’d done that once it became dangerously easy to tell Marley “Go for it” and approve whatever it had just put in my shopping cart. I watched it fill in my address details in the virtual browser window and confirmation emails started filing into my inbox. Marley did a little shopping around to find slightly better prices, and I didn’t buy anything egregious — just some descaling powder and water filters. It also did the math to calculate whether powdered Dezcal would be a better value than the liquid stuff (way better, not surprisingly). But it is shockingly easy to spend money when a cute little guy is running around the internet with your credit card. There’s a danger in overcommitting yourself when you feel like these AI tools are speeding you up. In a few cases, Muse helped me get started by putting the details I needed in front of my face. I had the phone number for the home security company at hand, as well as the name of my current plan and the one I wanted to downgrade to. Getting that little speed bump out of the way was what I needed, I guess. But the dirty secret of productivity hacks is that doing more stuff often doesn’t feel like things are being removed from your plate; somehow it just invites more tasks. If you’re willing to give a lot of information and trust to Meta — a massive caveat! — Muse can genuinely help you get things done. I’d been using it for all of 40 minutes and already given it my full name, address, credit card number, a photo of my backyard, and the credentials for my home security account login. Going great, I’d say! If AI decides to kill us all I just secured my spot at the front of the line. Meta of course says that all of these details are stored securely, Marley allegedly can’t even see them, etc., but still. Unsettling. But I think the underlying question we need to ask ourselves as we enter the era of AI agents is what we do with the time we’re supposedly freeing up. Will we use it to take on more commitments? And then ultimately feel overwhelmed again when the to-do list keeps piling up? After a morning crossing items off my list with Marley, I didn’t spend the hours that followed doing anything consequential. In fact, I spent that time chatting with Marley, seeking reassurance about the direction of the yard project and brainstorming fall camping trips I probably won’t take. It’s a gorgeous day outside, the kind we really can’t take for granted in late September, and I wish I’d spent that time outdoors rather than inside talking to a robot, cute little guy or otherwise. Photography by Allison Johnson / The Verge

articles.title: Anthropic says its biology lab has already found something big | TechCrunch
articles.summary: But maybe the biggest reveal is that Anthropic has not let Claude run loose in its biology lab. Humans are still, so far, in the loop.
articles.body:
Last week, Anthropic confirmed that it was operating a wet biology lab in the Bay Area where it uses its AI models to run physical experiments. This week, the AI giant announced that this lab has already made what it believes is a big discovery: a new enzyme “system” that has certain “properties reminiscent of CRISPR,” as Anthropic describes it .

CRISPR is a natural immune system used by bacteria to fight off viruses that has become a gene-editing technology widely used by researchers .

Essentially, what Anthropic says it found is a previously unknown enzyme system hidden in the DNA of bacteriophages, which are viruses that infect and replicate within bacteria. Anthropic’s researchers say this system behaves similarly to CRISPR in that it can “perform operations like cutting, copying, and pasting DNA.”

It will be up to the broader research community to validate how big, or new, this discovery actually is. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei acknowledges that the discovery was based on the work of others and that a team from Stanford previously discovered a system “that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found,” he wrote on X .

But Amodei and Anthropic are not just emphasizing the discovery. They are touting it was found “mostly, though not entirely, by Claude,” the CEO wrote.

On the one hand, that is astounding. This lab was only established this spring (though Anthropic declined to be more specific about how many months it has been open). A discovery in just a few short months would be speedy enough work, but the team said it actually only took Claude 21 hours of concerted effort. Claude searched through data using about 950 agents that burned through 210 million tokens.

Still, the revelation that Anthropic has been conducting biology experiments comes right after AI CEOs, including Amodei , publicly admitted that models have become so capable, and so potentially dangerous, that the industry must slow down and develop safety-testing procedures. This after a couple of his employees publicly said earlier this month that there’s a risk AI could kill us all .

Amodei himself has said one of the things he fears most is that AI could be used for bioterrorism. But he also believes AI will “cure most diseases in 5-10 years,” he wrote. So Anthropic has clearly decided the rewards are worth the risks.

Given that, perhaps the biggest reveal in this news isn’t the discovery itself but that the biology lab hasn’t let Claude loose. The physical experiments were done by humans.

“Our lab, located in the Bay Area, looks like a typical molecular biology lab. We do research that involves only the lower-levels of the biosafety risk level (BSL-1 and BSL-2) and we do not handle pathogens that can infect humans. All of the lab work is performed by human scientists.”

It’s also true that AI-powered biological research is hardly unique to Anthropic. Researchers from Stanford just published a paper on the work they are doing with LLMs and CRISPR. Researchers at UC San Francisco used AI to design enzymes from scratch . Google launched its first AI-powered biology research tool, AlphaFold, back in 2020 . So AI has clearly arrived in biological research beyond the AI labs pursuing it themselves.

Yet, Amodei hasn’t ruled out a fully automated biology lab in the future. “Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today,” he said.

articles.title: OpenAI, Anthropic bosses push UN for global terms on AI
articles.summary: OpenAI's Sam Altman has called for risk evaluation standards, as have Anthropic's Dario Amodei and Hugging Face's Clement Delangue.
articles.body:
The heads of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Hugging Face have told the UN that the current pace of artificial intelligence (AI) development, and the risks it poses to society, demands international coordination.

Altman called for common risk evaluation standards, as did Dario Amodei of Anthropic, a main rival of OpenAI, and Clement Delangue of Hugging Face.

Earlier this month, Amodei wrote an essay welcomed by Altman and others calling an AI development slowdown in response to fears about the technology's threat to humanity.

However, at the same UN conference, a key technology advisor to US President Donald Trump, rejected the idea any new form of AI regulation.

Michael Kratsios, a former Uber executive, admitted that the speed of AI development is increasing and that there are risks presented by the technology, but told the UN this was not reason enough "to pause development or constrain it with new global governance structures".

"International dialogue in this forum and others cannot be allowed to drift toward global governance," Kratsios added.

Kratsios's comments echoed similar statements made by Trump in recent weeks.

Trump told the UN on Tuesday he wanted to rebrand it "super intelligence" and has strongly opposed any idea of an AI slowdown because of the US's competitive advantage in the sector.

"We're leading China on AI... and, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins ," he said earlier this month.

Sam Altman of OpenAI and other AI chief executives expressed a different view in their talks to the UN on Wednesday.

"If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone," said Altman.

He told the UN that he wanted countries to start working together toward "the collective good in the face of powerful new technology".

He called for "national and international" AI standards on measuring the capabilities of an AI tool, assessing related risks, AI safeguards, and the degree to which human oversight over such tools is maintained.

He also called for "speedy incident reporting, classification, and reporting protocols so the world can learn from failures before they become catastrophes".

"We need common standards so countries can compare evidence, verify compliance, and have a shared language and understanding what is happening," Altman added.

Not all AI workers think the tech could kill everyone

AI 'kill switch' may need to be mandatory, Anthropic co-founder tells BBC

AI staff 'genuinely frightened' for humanity's future, ex-Anthropic researcher tells BBC

Anthropic's Amodei and Hugging Face's Delangue made similar comments in their speeches.

Amodei said that AI "if managed poorly... could be a risk to humanity as a whole".

He added that further development of AI tools calls for "even more stringent standards of safety".

"We will slow down as much as necessary in order to make sure that every successive AI technology that we release is actually safe," Amodei added.

"But regardless of what we do, managing these risks is ultimately bigger than any one company, and it has an industry-wide and global scale."

Hugging Face's Delangue said: "The global community needs stronger standards for monitoring and incident disclosure."

All three of the executives are based in the US and directly involved in the development of AI technology.

Hugging Face, a platform for AI developers, more recently rose to prominence after it admitted to being hacked by AI agents , or AI bots that operate somewhat autonomously, that came out of OpenAI.

Hugging Face has since been acquired by AI chipmaker Nvidia.

The Hugging Face hack has been treated as a 'wake-up call' within the industry for the ways in which AI technology has advanced and could hypothetically act in ways that could harm humanity.

articles.title: OpenAI agent 'infiltrated' Australian government website, PM says
articles.summary: Albanese said he expressed "concern" to OpenAI founder Sam Altman, after authorities were informed three months after the breach in June.
articles.body:
An artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI "infiltrated" an Australian government website in June, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has said.

The agent gained unauthorised accessed to a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive Medicare information", Albanese told a news conference at the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

Medicare refers to Australia's universal healthcare scheme. The breach is among the first publicly reported AI-led hacks of a government website in the world.

OpenAI said it only became aware of the incident in August "during an ongoing review of OpenAI misaligned model activity", and informed Australian officials on 10 September.

While the review is ongoing, a spokesperson for the AI firm said that it is not believed that any patient records were accessed.

Albanese said the breach occurred in June this year, but OpenAI only informed government officials via email on 10 September.

The prime minister said he spoke directly to CEO of OpenAI Sam Altman to say that it had taken "too long" to inform authorities and "to express Australia's extreme concern about this incident".

He said the agent accessed both public and non-public files and a "forensic investigation" is under way to find out if other government systems were affected.

The investigation will be led by the Australian Signals Directorate, the country's cybersecurity agency.

The public-facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal is administered by Services Australia, the main hub to redirect users to government services.

He told reporters: "No personal information is believed to have been accessed at this stage, but investigations are ongoing.

"Evidence currently available is there is no broader compromise to the Services Australia network. Nonetheless this situation is obviously unacceptable."

OpenAI gives cyber defence tools to Ukraine
